questions.stem: Which of the following is a biofuel?
options: Natural gas extracted from Bass Strait
Liquefied petroleum gas from crude oil
questions.explanation: Biodiesel is made from plant oils or animal fats, which can be regrown within a short time, so it is a biofuel. Liquefied petroleum gas, petrol and natural gas all come from fossil deposits that formed over millions of years, so they are fossil fuels.

questions.stem: In VCE Chemistry, a fuel is described as renewable when it:
options: has a higher energy content per gram than the fossil fuel it replaces
can be replaced by natural processes within a relatively short period of time
releases no carbon dioxide at all when it undergoes complete combustion
is produced from materials that were once living, as coal and petroleum are
questions.explanation: Renewability is about how quickly the resource is replaced by natural processes, which is why bioethanol from crops is renewable. Coal and petroleum did come from once-living organisms, but they took millions of years to form and are not replaced on a human timescale. Biofuels still release carbon dioxide when they burn.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of bioethanol compared with petrol as a transport fuel is that bioethanol:
options: releases less energy per gram when it undergoes complete combustion
is a fossil fuel that formed from ancient marine organisms over time
cannot be blended with petrol for use in ordinary car engines
produces sulfur dioxide as one of its main combustion products
questions.explanation: Ethanol already contains an oxygen atom, so it is partly oxidised and releases about 30 kJ g⁻¹ compared with about 48 kJ g⁻¹ for octane; a tank of ethanol takes a car less far. Bioethanol is made by fermenting plant sugars, so it is a biofuel, and it is routinely blended with petrol, as in E10.

questions.stem: Which component of food releases the most energy per gram when it is oxidised in the body?
questions.explanation: Fats and oils release about 37 kJ g⁻¹, more than twice the 16 kJ g⁻¹ of carbohydrates and 17 kJ g⁻¹ of proteins, because their molecules are long hydrocarbon chains with few oxygen atoms. Dietary fibre is largely undigested and supplies little energy.

questions.stem: A 40 g muesli bar contains 24 g of carbohydrate, 4 g of protein and 6 g of fat. Using 16, 17 and 37 kJ g⁻¹ respectively, what is its energy content?
questions.explanation: Energy = 24 × 16 + 4 × 17 + 6 × 37 = 384 + 68 + 222 = 674 kJ. Leaving out the fat gives 452 kJ, and treating the whole 40 g bar as carbohydrate gives 640 kJ; the remaining mass is water and fibre, which supply no energy here.

questions.stem: Photosynthesis is best described as a process that:
options: converts the chemical energy stored in glucose into light energy
releases carbon dioxide and water as its two main products
breaks down glucose to release energy for the plant's cells
converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose
questions.explanation: In photosynthesis, 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g), light energy is captured and stored as chemical energy in glucose. Breaking down glucose to release energy is cellular respiration, which uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water.

questions.stem: In cellular respiration, 9.00 g of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) is oxidised completely. What mass of oxygen is consumed?
questions.explanation: n(C₆H₁₂O₆) = 9.00 ÷ 180 = 0.0500 mol. The equation C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O needs 6 mol of oxygen per mole of glucose, so n(O₂) = 0.300 mol and m = 0.300 × 32.0 = 9.60 g. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 1.60 g, and 0.300 is the amount in moles, not a mass.

questions.stem: After fermentation, bioethanol is present as a dilute solution in water. Which process concentrates it for use as a fuel, and why does it work?
options: Chromatography, because ethanol is more soluble in water than glucose
Distillation, because ethanol has a lower boiling point than water
Filtration, because ethanol molecules are smaller than water molecules
Distillation, because ethanol has a higher boiling point than water
questions.explanation: Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C, so heating the mixture vaporises ethanol preferentially and the condensed distillate is richer in ethanol. Filtration separates solids from liquids, not two miscible liquids, and ethanol's boiling point is lower, not higher, than water's.

questions.stem: Glucose ferments: C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2CO₂(g). What volume of carbon dioxide, measured at SLC, is produced from 360 g of glucose?
questions.explanation: n(C₆H₁₂O₆) = 360 ÷ 180 = 2.00 mol, so n(CO₂) = 2 × 2.00 = 4.00 mol and V = 4.00 × 24.8 = 99.2 L at SLC. Forgetting the 2 : 1 ratio gives 49.6 L, and 89.6 L uses 22.4 L mol⁻¹, the molar volume at 0 °C, not at SLC.

questions.stem: In an exothermic reaction:
options: energy is released as the bonds in the reactants break, which gives the reaction a negative ΔH
the products hold more chemical energy than the reactants, which gives the reaction a negative ΔH
more energy is released forming bonds in the products than is absorbed breaking bonds in the reactants
more energy is absorbed breaking bonds in the reactants than is released forming bonds in the products
questions.explanation: Breaking bonds always absorbs energy and making bonds always releases it; a reaction is exothermic when the energy released by bond making exceeds that absorbed by bond breaking. The products then have less chemical energy than the reactants and ΔH is negative.

questions.stem: On an energy profile diagram for an endothermic reaction, the products are drawn:
options: higher than the reactants, and ΔH is negative
level with the peak, and ΔH equals the activation energy
higher than the reactants, and ΔH is positive
lower than the reactants, and ΔH is positive
questions.explanation: In an endothermic reaction the system absorbs energy, so the products have more enthalpy than the reactants and ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) is positive. The peak represents the activation energy, which is the energy needed to reach the transition state, not the enthalpy of the products.

questions.stem: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹. How much energy is released per gram of methane burnt?
questions.explanation: M(CH₄) = 16.0 g mol⁻¹, so energy per gram = 890 ÷ 16.0 = 55.6 kJ g⁻¹. 890 kJ is the energy per mole, and multiplying by the molar mass instead of dividing gives about 14 200 kJ g⁻¹.

questions.stem: 4.0 g of hydrogen and 16.0 g of oxygen are ignited: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l). Which statement is correct?
options: Hydrogen is limiting and 36.0 g of water forms
Oxygen is limiting and 18.0 g of water forms
Hydrogen is limiting and 18.0 g of water forms
Oxygen is limiting and 36.0 g of water forms
questions.explanation: n(H₂) = 4.0 ÷ 2.0 = 2.0 mol and n(O₂) = 16.0 ÷ 32.0 = 0.500 mol. Burning all the hydrogen would need 1.0 mol of oxygen, so oxygen is limiting; it forms 2 × 0.500 = 1.00 mol of water, which is 18.0 g. 36.0 g would form only if all the hydrogen reacted.

questions.stem: 11.0 g of propane burns in 32.0 g of oxygen: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l), ΔH = −2220 kJ mol⁻¹. How much heat is released?
questions.explanation: n(C₃H₈) = 11.0 ÷ 44.0 = 0.250 mol, which needs 1.25 mol of oxygen, but only 32.0 ÷ 32.0 = 1.00 mol is present. Oxygen is limiting, so 1.00 ÷ 5 = 0.200 mol of propane reacts and releases 0.200 × 2220 = 444 kJ. 555 kJ assumes all the propane burns.

questions.stem: Incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel occurs when:
options: the fuel contains impurities, producing sulfur dioxide instead of water
the flame is very hot, so the fuel breaks into hydrogen and carbon dioxide
the oxygen supply is limited, producing carbon monoxide or carbon (soot)
oxygen is in excess, producing only carbon dioxide and water vapour
questions.explanation: With too little oxygen, not all the carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide, so carbon monoxide and soot form and less energy is released. Excess oxygen gives complete combustion. Sulfur impurities do produce sulfur dioxide, but that happens in either kind of combustion and is not what makes it incomplete.

questions.stem: Which balanced equation represents the incomplete combustion of ethanol to form carbon monoxide?
questions.explanation: Counting oxygen atoms: 1 in ethanol plus 4 in 2O₂ gives 5, matching 2 in 2CO and 3 in 3H₂O. The equation with 3O₂ forming carbon dioxide is balanced but shows complete combustion. The doubled equation has 12 oxygen atoms on the left and only 10 on the right.

questions.stem: When 1.00 g of octane (M = 114 g mol⁻¹) burns completely, 47.9 kJ of heat is released. Which thermochemical equation is correct?
questions.explanation: Per mole, 47.9 × 114 = 5.46 × 10³ kJ, and the equation as written burns 2 mol of octane, so ΔH = −2 × 5.46 × 10³ = −1.09 × 10⁴ kJ mol⁻¹. Using −5.46 × 10³ with the doubled equation ignores the coefficient, and combustion is exothermic, so ΔH is negative.

questions.stem: Propane burns: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l). At SLC, what volume of oxygen is needed to burn 10.0 L of propane completely?
questions.explanation: At the same temperature and pressure, equal amounts in moles of gases occupy equal volumes, so volumes react in the mole ratio of the equation: 5 × 10.0 = 50.0 L of oxygen. 30.0 L is the volume of carbon dioxide produced, not the oxygen needed.

questions.stem: A car burns 2.28 kg of octane (M = 114 g mol⁻¹) completely: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O. What mass of carbon dioxide is released?
questions.explanation: n(C₈H₁₈) = 2280 ÷ 114 = 20.0 mol, and each mole gives 8 mol of carbon dioxide, so n(CO₂) = 160 mol and m = 160 × 44.0 = 7040 g = 7.04 kg. A 1 : 1 ratio gives 0.880 kg. The mass of carbon dioxide exceeds the fuel's mass because oxygen from the air is added.

questions.stem: Methane burns: ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹. What mass of carbon dioxide is released when methane burns completely to supply 1.00 × 10³ kJ of heat?
questions.explanation: n(CH₄) = 1000 ÷ 890 = 1.12 mol, and each mole of methane gives 1 mol of carbon dioxide, so m(CO₂) = 1.12 × 44.0 = 49.4 g. 18.0 g is the mass of methane burnt, not of carbon dioxide formed, and 98.9 g wrongly uses the 2 : 1 ratio that belongs to water.

questions.stem: Taking c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, how much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 200 g of water by 15.0 °C?
questions.explanation: q = mcΔT = 200 × 4.18 × 15.0 = 12 540 J = 12.5 kJ. A change of 15.0 °C is the same as a change of 15.0 K. Leaving the answer in joules but labelling it kJ gives 12 540 kJ, a thousand times too large.

questions.stem: A spirit burner heats 250 g of water from 20.0 °C to 45.0 °C while losing 1.50 g of ethanol. Assuming all the heat reaches the water, what is the heat of combustion of ethanol?
questions.explanation: q = 250 × 4.18 × 25.0 = 26 125 J = 26.1 kJ, and dividing by the 1.50 g burnt gives 17.4 kJ g⁻¹. 26.1 kJ is the total heat, not the heat per gram, and 39.2 comes from multiplying by the mass instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A student's value for the heat of combustion of ethanol from a spirit burner is well below the data book value. What is the most likely main cause?
options: The specific heat capacity of water rises sharply as the water warms up
Burning with a sooty yellow flame made the ethanol release extra energy
Heat was lost to the air and the can instead of being absorbed by the water
The water absorbed more heat than the burning ethanol actually released
questions.explanation: In an open spirit-burner set-up much of the heat escapes to the air, the can and the thermometer, so the water's temperature rise, and the calculated value, is too low. A sooty flame indicates incomplete combustion, which releases less energy, not more. Water's specific heat capacity barely changes between 20 °C and 45 °C.

questions.stem: In solution calorimetry, the calibration factor is:
options: the temperature rise produced when 1 mol of the reactant dissolves in the water
the electrical current needed to keep the calorimeter at a constant temperature
the energy needed to raise the temperature of the calorimeter and its contents by 1 °C
the energy released per gram of the substance that reacts inside the calorimeter
questions.explanation: The calibration factor, in J °C⁻¹, accounts for all the parts that absorb heat, including the water, cup, stirrer and thermometer. It is found by adding a known amount of energy, usually electrically, and measuring the temperature rise. Energy per gram is what the experiment then measures, using the calibration factor.

questions.stem: A calorimeter is calibrated by passing a current of 4.50 A at 6.00 V for 120 s, and the temperature rises by 2.40 °C. What is its calibration factor?
questions.explanation: E = VIt = 6.00 × 4.50 × 120 = 3240 J, and CF = E ÷ ΔT = 3240 ÷ 2.40 = 1350 J °C⁻¹ = 1.35 kJ °C⁻¹. 3.24 kJ is the energy supplied, not the energy per degree, and 11.3 J °C⁻¹ leaves out the time.

questions.stem: A calorimeter has a calibration factor of 1.35 kJ °C⁻¹. When 0.0500 mol of a salt dissolves in it, the temperature rises by 3.00 °C. What is ΔH for the dissolution?
questions.explanation: Energy released = 1.35 × 3.00 = 4.05 kJ, and per mole this is 4.05 ÷ 0.0500 = 81.0 kJ mol⁻¹. The temperature rose, so heat was released to the solution and ΔH is negative. −4.05 kJ is the energy for 0.0500 mol, not per mole.

questions.stem: In solution calorimetry, why is the cooling part of the temperature–time graph extrapolated back to the time of mixing?
options: To estimate the temperature rise that would have occurred with no heat loss
To find the moment at which the reaction reached its activation energy
To determine the calibration factor without passing an electric current
To find the temperature of the water before the solid was weighed out
questions.explanation: Heat is lost to the surroundings while the reaction proceeds, so the highest reading underestimates the true rise. Extrapolating the cooling line back to the moment of mixing corrects for that loss. The calibration factor still has to be measured separately, by electrical or chemical calibration.

questions.stem: A gas heater burns 0.500 mol of methane (ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹) and 312 kJ of heat is absorbed by the water. What is the energy transformation efficiency?
questions.explanation: Chemical energy released = 0.500 × 890 = 445 kJ, so efficiency = 312 ÷ 445 × 100 = 70.1%. 35.1% compares the useful energy with 1 mol of methane rather than the 0.500 mol burnt, and 29.9% is the percentage wasted.

questions.stem: A 2.00 g almond is burnt beneath a can holding 100 g of water, which warms by 24.0 °C. The label says almonds contain 25.0 kJ g⁻¹. What percentage of the almond's energy reached the water?
questions.explanation: Energy absorbed = 100 × 4.18 × 24.0 = 10 032 J = 10.0 kJ. The almond holds 2.00 × 25.0 = 50.0 kJ, so efficiency = 10.0 ÷ 50.0 × 100 = 20.1%. Comparing with the energy of only 1 g gives 40.1%.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of manganese in the permanganate ion, MnO₄−?
questions.explanation: Each oxygen is −2, so four oxygens contribute −8, and the ion's overall charge is −1: x + (−8) = −1, giving x = +7. +8 ignores the ion's charge, and −1 is the charge of the whole ion, not of manganese.

questions.stem: Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s). Which statement is correct?
options: Copper(II) ions are the reducing agent and are reduced
Copper(II) ions are oxidised because they gain electrons
Zinc is the reducing agent and is oxidised
Zinc is the oxidising agent and is oxidised
questions.explanation: Zinc's oxidation number rises from 0 to +2, so it loses electrons and is oxidised; the species that is oxidised is the reducing agent. Copper(II) ions gain electrons and are reduced, which makes them the oxidising agent.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a conjugate redox pair?
questions.explanation: A conjugate redox pair is an oxidising agent and the reducing agent it becomes after gaining electrons: Fe3+ + e− → Fe2+. Fe2+ and Cu2+ are different elements, and Cl₂ and Br− are too. H+ and OH− are linked by acid–base chemistry, not by electron transfer.

questions.stem: Which half-equation is correctly balanced for the reduction of permanganate ions in acidic conditions?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is balanced with 4H₂O, hydrogen with 8H+, and charge with electrons: −1 + 8 − 5 = +2 on the left matches +2 on the right. Electrons appear on the left because manganese is reduced from +7 to +2. With 3e− the charges are +4 and +2, and 4H+ leaves hydrogen unbalanced.

questions.stem: Which half-equation shows the oxidation of hydrogen gas in a fuel cell with an alkaline electrolyte?
questions.explanation: In basic conditions H+ is not a significant species, so hydrogen reacts with hydroxide ions, and charge balances: −2 on the left, 0 − 2 = −2 on the right. Forming H+ is the half-equation in acidic conditions. With electrons on the left the charges no longer balance, and the version with one OH− leaves hydrogen unbalanced.

questions.stem: In a galvanic cell, the anode is:
questions.explanation: Oxidation always occurs at the anode. In a galvanic cell, the oxidation releases electrons into the anode, giving it an excess of electrons and a negative polarity; electrons flow through the external circuit to the positive cathode, where reduction occurs.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell has Zn/Zn2+ and Cu/Cu2+ half-cells joined by a salt bridge of KNO₃ solution. While the cell operates:
options: nitrate ions migrate towards the copper half-cell
potassium ions migrate towards the zinc half-cell
nitrate ions migrate towards the zinc half-cell
electrons travel through the salt bridge to copper
questions.explanation: Zinc is oxidised, adding Zn2+ ions to its half-cell, so anions from the salt bridge flow in to balance the charge; cations flow towards the copper half-cell, where Cu2+ ions are removed. Electrons travel only through the external wire, never through the solution.

questions.stem: A half-cell contains Fe3+(aq) and Fe2+(aq) ions. Why is an inert electrode such as graphite used in it?
options: Graphite is oxidised more readily than Fe2+ ions, so it acts as the anode
Graphite reacts with Fe3+ ions, and this reaction produces the current
Iron metal cannot conduct electrons while it sits in a solution of its own ions
Neither species is a solid metal, so an inert conductor must carry the electrons
questions.explanation: Both members of the conjugate pair are dissolved ions, so the half-cell needs a solid conductor that transfers electrons without reacting itself. Graphite or platinum does this. An inert electrode takes no part in the redox reaction, so it is neither oxidised nor a source of the current.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Ag+/Ag (E° = +0.80 V) and Ni2+/Ni (E° = −0.25 V) half-cells under standard conditions. Which statement is correct?
options: The maximum voltage is 1.05 V and nickel is the anode
The maximum voltage is 0.55 V and nickel is the anode
The maximum voltage is 1.05 V and silver is the anode
The maximum voltage is 0.55 V and silver is the anode
questions.explanation: The maximum cell voltage is the difference between the E° values: 0.80 − (−0.25) = 1.05 V. Silver ions are the stronger oxidising agent and are reduced at the cathode, so nickel is oxidised at the anode. Adding the two values gives 0.55 V, which ignores the sign.

questions.stem: E° values: Cl₂/Cl− +1.36 V, Br₂/Br− +1.09 V, I₂/I− +0.54 V. Which mixture reacts spontaneously?
options: Chlorine water added to potassium bromide solution
Iodine solution added to potassium bromide solution
Bromine water added to potassium chloride solution
Iodine solution added to potassium chloride solution
questions.explanation: A reaction is predicted when the oxidising agent sits higher in the electrochemical series than the reducing agent. Chlorine (+1.36 V) is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine, so it oxidises Br− to Br₂. Bromine and iodine are weaker oxidising agents than chlorine, so they cannot oxidise Cl−, and iodine cannot oxidise Br−.

questions.stem: The electrochemical series predicts that a metal should react with a solution, but no change is seen after several minutes. What is the best explanation?
options: The series shows whether a reaction can occur, not how fast it occurs
A large difference in E° values means the reaction happens very slowly
The species higher in the series is the stronger reducing agent, so it reverses
E° values are measured against a copper half-cell, so they mislead here
questions.explanation: E° values indicate whether a reaction is energetically favourable under standard conditions; they say nothing about rate, and some predicted reactions are too slow to observe. Non-standard concentrations or temperatures can also change the outcome. Standard electrode potentials are measured against the standard hydrogen half-cell, not copper.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a fuel cell from a primary galvanic cell?
options: Its reactants are sealed inside when it is made
Its reactants are supplied continuously from outside
It converts electrical energy into chemical energy
Oxidation in it occurs at the positive electrode
questions.explanation: A fuel cell keeps producing electricity as long as fuel and oxidant are fed in, whereas a primary cell stops when its stored reactants are used up. Both are galvanic cells, converting chemical energy into electrical energy, with oxidation at the negative anode.

questions.stem: Why do fuel cells use porous electrodes?
options: They keep the gases away from the catalyst until power is needed
They give a large area where gas, electrolyte and catalyst meet
They let the electrolyte drain away so the cell stays dry
They let electrons pass from the anode through the electrolyte
questions.explanation: Gaseous reactants diffuse into the pores, giving a large surface where the gas, the electrolyte and the catalyst on the electrode are in contact, which raises the rate and the cell's efficiency. Electrons always travel through the external circuit, never through the electrolyte.

questions.stem: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte delivers 2.00 A for 9650 s. Taking F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹, what mass of hydrogen is consumed?
questions.explanation: Q = It = 2.00 × 9650 = 19 300 C, so n(e−) = 19 300 ÷ 96 500 = 0.200 mol. At the anode H₂ → 2H+ + 2e−, so n(H₂) = 0.100 mol and m = 0.100 × 2.0 = 0.200 g. 0.100 g is the amount in moles mistaken for a mass, and 0.0500 g uses the 4 electrons that belong to oxygen.

questions.stem: Fuel cells convert the chemical energy of a fuel to electrical energy more efficiently than a power station burning the same fuel. Why?
options: They turn heat into electricity without any energy being wasted
The energy is converted directly, without first being turned into heat
Their reactions release more energy per mole of fuel than burning does
They need no catalyst, so no energy is lost activating the reaction
questions.explanation: A power station converts chemical energy to heat, then to mechanical energy, then to electricity, losing energy at each step. A fuel cell converts chemical energy straight to electrical energy. The overall energy change for a given reaction is the same either way, and fuel cells do use catalysts on their electrodes.

questions.stem: A fuel cell plant switches from hydrogen made from natural gas to hydrogen made from biogas produced from food waste. Which green chemistry principle does this most directly apply?
questions.explanation: Biogas comes from organic waste that is replaced on a short timescale, so the feedstock is renewable, whereas natural gas is a finite fossil resource. Design for energy efficiency concerns reducing the energy a process uses, which this change does not directly address.
